External links for this lesson. All checked to load from a plain request as of the date this
page was written. (Note: eCFR's own site — ecfr.gov — blocks automated/proxied traffic with a
bot check in this repo's build environment, even though a human browser reaches it fine; the
regulation text quoted in this lesson comes from eCFR's public Versioner API instead, and the
links below use verified-loading mirrors of the same official text.)

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 610.40, current text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/610.40)**
  — Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute mirror of the infectious-disease test
  requirements quoted throughout this lesson, including the release-restriction and reactive-
  result provisions. Use this to check the current text, since the copy in this repo's `sources/`
  folder is a dated snapshot.

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 606.40, current text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/606.40)**
  — the facilities regulation that requires a designated quarantine storage location, quoted in
  this lesson's "actual text" section. Same use case: check for amendments against the dated
  snapshot in `sources/`.

- **[Cornell LII: Title 21, Part 610 browse index](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/part-610)**
  — the full general biological product standards part this lesson's testing citation sits
  inside, including § 610.41 (donor deferral on a reactive result) and § 610.46–.47 (lookback
  and consignee notification procedures), which this director-level lesson names but doesn't
  quote — your Quality Analyst will cite these directly when a reactive result actually occurs.

- **[GovInfo: Code of Federal Regulations](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/collection/cfr)** — the
  U.S. Government Publishing Office's official, legally authoritative annual CFR archive. Use
  this for the official, dated, legally citable version of a specific year's text — for example,
  to confirm exactly what 610.40 said on the date of a past inspection or a reactive-result
  investigation.

- **[What Really Happens to Your Blood After You
  Donate?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oZwtv9IJH6A)** (Seeker, from oEmbed `author_name`). This is
  the science-education explainer embedded in the lesson. It isn't FDA/CFR-specific, so don't treat any
  number or procedure it shows as governed by 606/610. The operational shape (split fast, test in
  parallel, hold until clear) is what maps onto this lesson. Verified embeddable via YouTube oEmbed on
  2026-11-13 (HTTP 200).

- **[AABB: Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and
  Components](https://www.aabb.org/news-resources/resources/circular-of-information)** — the
  official joint blood-community reference (published through AABB) that actually states
  each component's shelf life, storage temperature, and indications for use: what red cells,
  plasma, and platelets each need once they're split apart Tuesday afternoon, the detail this
  lesson names ("very different shelf lives") but doesn't itself spell out. Verified loading via
  `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[Microsoft Learn: Deployment gates concepts — Azure
  Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates)**
  — a concrete, non-blood-industry explainer of the exact ITSM concept this lesson's bridge
  leans on: a gate that automatically checks required conditions before anything is allowed to
  release, independent of how far along the pipeline already is. Read 610.40(g)/(h)(1)'s
  release gate through this lens, then notice where the blood-center version is stricter — a
  failed gate here triggers donor deferral and notification, not just a blocked deployment.
  Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

## Keep learning

Not official sources — good places to learn more about collection, quarantine, and infectious-disease testing in practice.

- **[BBGuy Essentials 003: septic transfusion reactions with Dr. Anne Eder (transcript, PDF)](https://www.bbguy.org/pdf/BBGE_003_Anne_Eder_Transcript.pdf)** (Blood Bank Guy podcast) — why bacterial contamination of platelets is a distinct testing problem from viral screening. The conversation predates later FDA guidance, so treat the testing details as history, not current practice. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200; PDF, no HTML title).
